problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1?$

activity_context.topic_title: Line Integrals of Scalar Functions Over Circles

feedback.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{3},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=36?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $6$ centered at $(1,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={y}^{3},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }((6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)^{3})\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
